title: Reverse-lookup service exposed millions of photos of people's faces
gist: People-search site ClarityCheck left about 450GB and over 9 million face photos publicly exposed in an unsecured S3 bucket for months, plus a separate flaw exposing contact data via URL manipulation, highlighting structural, non-diversifiable breach risk across the data-broker industry.

insights.claim: Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler found that people-search site ClarityCheck left roughly 450GB and over 9 million image files -- including face photos of adults, teens, and children -- publicly exposed in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket accessible via a URL embedded in the company's own public website code, for a period of months before being secured after WIRED contacted the company in July 2026.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Another concrete case of a data-broker company mishandling biometric data at scale; relevant to growing regulatory and litigation risk facing the people-search industry as state biometric privacy laws expand.
insights.locator: the exposed ClarityCheck database contained roughly 450 GB of images

insights.claim: A second ClarityCheck misconfiguration allowed anyone to manipulate website URLs by entering names to retrieve multiple people's email addresses, physical addresses, and phone numbers without authentication; both flaws were fixed only after WIRED's outreach, and Fowler's earlier direct attempts to report the issue to the company had been unsuccessful.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Highlights weak vulnerability-disclosure and response processes as a recurring failure mode among data-broker companies, a due-diligence red flag for any investor or partner evaluating such firms.
insights.locator: his initial efforts to flag the problem to the company were unsuccessful

insights.claim: ClarityCheck disputes the 'exposed' characterization, arguing the data sat behind an unindexed URL not discoverable through ordinary search, but security experts state that data reachable without authentication constitutes exposure regardless of whether it has been actively discovered, indicating an unresolved definitional dispute over what counts as a breach.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: This disclosure-semantics dispute recurs across breach-notification cases and affects whether companies face legal or regulatory breach-notification obligations -- a relevant framework for assessing future incident disclosures in this sector.
insights.quote: Exposure is the state in which personal or sensitive data has been left accessible, discoverable, or otherwise put at risk of unauthorized access, whether or not anyone has yet taken or misused it. A publicly reachable database backup, a misconfigured storage bucket, or credentials sitting in a system that a researcher can reach are all exposures.
insights.locator: says Mark Beare, head of consumer products at the security company Malwarebytes

insights.claim: Because face images are permanent, unchangeable biometric identifiers unlike passwords, researchers warn that exposed face databases carry structurally higher long-term risk than typical credential leaks, including potential unauthorized use for AI facial-recognition model training or for building synthetic 'catfishing' personas from scraped photos.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Underscores that biometric-data breaches carry longer-duration, non-remediable risk compared to typical password or credential leaks.
insights.quote: Let's say I was in a criminal outfit and I was catfishing people, and I scroll through all these pictures and I pick out 20 of the most attractive people and then I just use their image and AI and I create a persona

insights.claim: ClarityCheck's business model is built on collecting and exposing exactly this kind of sensitive biometric and PII data by design, per the ACLU's Rebecca Williams, meaning stronger data-minimization and security practices cannot fully eliminate breach risk for this category of company because the underlying business model requires amassing sensitive personal data at scale.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A structural argument that people-search and identity-verification companies carry inherent, non-diversifiable data-breach risk tied directly to their core business model, relevant to risk assessment of the entire data-broker sector.
insights.quote: Systems that rely on highly sensitive personal information to verify individuals will continue to carry these risks, even with stronger data minimization and security practices, because the model itself depends on collecting sensitive data
insights.locator: says Rebecca Williams, director of strategy for privacy and data governance at the American Civil Liberties Union
